name: Rabi'ah ibn Maqrum
bio: Rabi'ah ibn Maqrum, of Dabbah, the tribe of al-Mufaddal himself, was taken prisoner by the Persian King and later became a Muslim, fighting at the battles of Qadisiyah (A.H. 15) and Jalula. Lyall reports that he reached a great age.
The pieces by him in the Mufaddaliyat celebrate his own or his tribe's warlike deeds.

poems.title: Ode XXXVIII: Hast thou recognized the traces of
poems.author: Rabi'ah ibn Maqrum
poems.note: Lyall's heading: Rabi'ah son of Maqrum, of the family of Ghaidh son of as-Sid, of Dabbah.
poems.text:
Hast thou recognized the traces of the household of Hind in Jumran — now void, but they will not vanish?

Thou Wouldst deem the lines, known once so well, now that two years have passed, were patterns tattooed.

I stayed my camel there while I questioned them— but to what purpose asked I aught of the traces?

The marks of her dwelling stirred memories of her, and memory kindled to longing a sick heart,

And my tears flowed fast, though I strove to stay them, over my beard and my raiment in streams.

Then I turned away from the spot a light-coloured camel, fleet as a wild-ass, strong and sturdy, that is never tired of pushing on,

Close and firm of flesh, like a male in strength: when other camels whimper with distress, thou seest her silent.

'Twas as though I had fastened her belly-girths round a slender-waisted [wild-ass] with a white patch on his flank, stout in frame, repellent in aspect.

He keeps away from the water three mates, lean like lances, and prevents them from drinking in spite of raging thirst.

He pastured them on the dry uplands until the herbage of the hollows where water stood had quite dried up, and he dreaded the deadly hot wind.

And they stood day-long with parched throats, watching the sun with eyes contracted, in fear lest they should faint from thirst.

Then, when he was convinced that day had quite departed, and he perceived that it was now black unbroken night,

He threw them into the midst of the darkness, galloping alongside — a biter, a thruster, snapping at them with his teeth.

And he brought them down at the first flush of dawn to the springs that cast forth from them all rubbish [borne upon them by the wind],

Spouting upwards, deep blue like the sky in colour — they see therein the glittering points of the stars.

And by the water is Qais the father of 'Amir: he gives them time for a space to stand there ;

In his hand is a bow of wood grown in the Haram, made of a whole branch : [when pulled,] there follows the hiss [of the arrow] a resounding twang,

And a slender arrow, pared down fine, on whose stem thou mayst see a stain of blood which has sunk into it.

But he missed them, and all of them fled away, almost bursting their skins in affright.

And if thou askest of me, know that I am a man who holds the mean in contempt, and heaps gifts on the noble.

I build up high renown by mighty deeds, and I feed full the needy, and pour wine to my boon-fellow ;

And he who seeks for bounty praises my liberality to him, what time the seeker blames the mean for his niggardliness.

And I pay my debts faithfully and fully — my evil for evil, my good for good.

And my people — if thou doubtest what I say, then ask of my people one who knows them —

Whether they are not, when the jaws of Famine bite hard upon men, causing them to forget their dignity,

Folk who hold lightly their goods in the face of claims on them, when distress wears away the means of the owner of cattle.

Long are their spears on the morning of the dawn-attack : valorous are they, protectors of their women and babes,

Children of War on a day when they clothe themselves in mail — thou wouldst think them stallion-camels clad in iron.

My house be their sacrifice for what they did at Buzakhah when they filled with their hosts the upland plain !

And [what they did] when 'Amir at an-Nisar and at Tikhfah met at their hands with a disastrous day :

[At an-Nisar] they forced the whole tribe of Hawazin to yield them the half of their possessions, the rich and the poor of them alike.

And against us Madhhij at al-Kulab led their forces, all their confederates as well as their own pure stock :

There our war-mill whirled, grinding down their horsemen, and they became rotten bones, as though they had never been,

With spear-thrusts wherefrom the spouting blood gushed forth, and sword-strokes that clove the skull down to the shoulders ;

And their bodies in Taiman lay so thickly together, that he who saw them would liken them to fallen leaves of trees.

We left 'Umarah among the spears — 'Umarah of 'Abs, wounded and drained of blood ;

And but for our horsemen, Tamlm, on the Day of Dhat as-Sulaim, had not raised the war-cry of Tamim.

It is not to cast shame upon Tamlm that I count up the great deeds of my people, or to blame them at all,

But I am calling to mind only the benefits we conferred on them, both those of late date and those of long ago.

And many the place of indignity we have disdained to dwell in, and instead thereof have pitched in a glorious camping-place,

What time many a man dwelt with Contempt as a trusty yoke-fellow and a tender mother.

And many the dreaded breach where we stood as its defenders, when all except us shrank in fear from standing there;

We made our bulwarks there our swords and our spears and the mail-coats of iron rings strung together,

And short-haired steeds, preferred to our children in nurture —in the midst of our tents they champ their bits :

They are accustomed in war not to yield their place : when they are wounded, they make no complaint of their wounds.

poems.title: Ode XXXIX: Ar-Ruwa' has cast off affection for
poems.author: Rabi'ah ibn Maqrum
poems.text:
Ar-Ruwa' has cast off affection for thee, and determined on separation from thee and farewell.

And she said, ' What is he now but a worn-out old man ? ' and repulsion was strong in her, and she sought not to overcome it.

Yea, and if [through advancing years] I have come back to my senses, and a veil of hoary hair gleams white o'er my brow,

Yet I know how to cleave close to a friend though he be far from me, and the fruit, of hating me is an unwholesome pasture.

And I guard, though they be absent, the cause of my tribe, and it is not neglected with me, nor is it lost.

And through me the poor starveling is made happy when he seeks me : but the valiant fighter mislikes entering on a contest with me.

And it stops the voice of blame that I am [admitted by all to be] noble, and that the place of my dwelling is high upon the mountain for all to see,

And that I am obeyed among the Children of Bakr son of Sa'd, what time all their scattered companies are gathered together.

And many [the host of horse] whose flanks were closely compacted, great in multitude, moving along with its spear-heads shining in the sun,

At whose attack I have been present, and have stood my ground therein, what time the pithless weakling quaked with affright.

And many the stubborn adversary, difficult to handle, ready to distort anything from the truth, whose sole object to be grasped at was to hurl at me revilings,

Obstinate like a horse jerking upwards his head, to whom I have been a bit to tame him, and a bandage to blind his eyes :

When he wriggled and struggled, he was straightened out by the force of adversity and by crushing blows, so that the raging veins in his neck calmed down.

And many the shag-pated waif whose kin have turned away from him, a castaway like an old saddle-cloth, with no force of resolve or energy left,

A wretch full of misery, to whom I have brought happiness once more, so that into his life spaciousness has returned again.

And many the water, its depths corrupt through long loneliness, in a solitary wilderness, round whose sides the beasts of prey wander to and fro,

I have visited, what time the Pleiads had dropped to their setting, while under my saddle-pad was a big-framed long-stepping camel,

Stout and muscular, that moves the upper part of his forelegs to and fro, and speeds along upon nimble shanks set in a well-knit frame.

He has a ring in his nose which, when he presses sideways out of the course, pulls his neck round, and the spinal cord of his neck becomes soft in consequence.

It seems as though his saddle were bound upon a sturdy wild-ass, who has found the grazing in the water-courses of Ma'qulah to his mind —

Water-courses coming down from upland meadows well soaked by successive showers that have fallen under the constellation of the Ram.

He has become therefrom stout and well knit together, like a cable of palm-fibre the loosely-laid strands of which have been rolled close together by a skilful Syrian woman.

He turns hither and thither a long-bodied she-ass, long of neck, whose body-hair flies about in the wind, and in her are streaks of white [like the gores in a shirt].

When the two came down into the plain, she gained somewhat upon him in their running : but in spite of her boldness, he kept closely up to her ;

He turned away from the drinking-places of the valley of Qaww, and the broken rugged path towards the Harrah did away with her superiority in speed ;

And the nearest watering-place where they arrived, at the setting-in of night, was Uthal, or Ghumazah, or Nuta'.

And he brought her down to drink when the night was one pitch-darkness, and the twain were nowise weary when the dawn broke upon them.

But with the dawn he lighted on a serpent of the Children of Jillan, whose only gear was his bent bow and his arrows :

When he slaughters not for his children fresh juicy meat of the foremost of the wildings, they have to go hungry.

So he let fly at them an arrow, slender, with its head worn down on both sides by sharpening — but a breaking of the bow-string caused him to miss the shot !

And he cried Woe upon his mother, while [the wild ass] sped away at headlong speed, about him a cloud of dust from his galloping, spreading in the air.

poems.title: Ode XLIII: Su'ad is gone, and thy heart
poems.author: Rabi'ah ibn Maqrum
poems.text:
Su'ad is gone, and thy heart lies sick with fever of love ; the freeman's Daughter has left her pledges all unfulfilled.

A young gazelle is she like, unmated, grazing her fill where torrent-channels are green in hollow Haumal or Ud.

That morning we parted, she stood, her tresses fallen unbound, that hung like clusters of black grapes all adown her back :

Her [ruddy mouth] cool and fair, most sweet to kiss, with a row of ordered teeth, not too close, all lustrous, honey to taste.

Yea, many a strong camel, spare of frame, lean, bleeding her pads, have I pushed on without stint to bear me over the wastes ;

I laid this load on her — well she bore it, as but her due — to face a fierce melting heat that burnt like blazing flame :

A desert waterless, wide, wherein is death to be feared — all night unwearied its owls hoot on with never a break.

When she complained of sore travel, this my word in reply : ' Thou shalt not rest till I come to see the face of Mas'ud—

Until I look on the man whose gifts are boundless, his tent open to all who have need, his arm long, praised of all men.

Yea, many men have I heard lauded above all their kind, but never heard of thy like in gracious bountifulness,

Nor yet in temperance, nor in patience when trouble fell — nay, no vain words do I use to tell the Sid of thy fame !

Thy gracious manner is not the grace that stirs men's ire, nor is thy bounty refused to any seeker that comes.

Thou readiest, foremost of all, the goals set up for the best, and thou resemblest thy fathers, high-headed lords of men.

This is my praise for the fair gifts showered by thee on me : mayst thou ne'er cease to be happy and envied by all men !

poems.title: Ode CXIII: Thou callest Zainab to mind, and
poems.author: Rabi'ah ibn Maqrum
poems.text:
Thou callest Zainab to mind, and the thought of her stirs thy heart : but all the remnant of union with her was sundered long ago ;

And our people dwell in Falj and al-Abatir, while she has gone far away, to live in Ghamrah, and then in Muthaqqab.

And if thou seest that I have given over my ardour in pursuit, and have become white in the cheeks and hoary-headed,

And am meek to the bidding of censorious ones — and" time was when I appeared to them stubborn of soul, a stirrer-up of strife —

Yet in the past how many an active adversary have I been able to repel, and have bent his crookedness straight so that he shunned my company !

And many the kinsman I have helped, though strait was the place where he stood, when the weakling's fire-stick gave no spark, and he wavered this way and that ;

And many the guests of the night, when the chill north wind was blowing, have I regaled with juicy slices of the hump of good fat camels ;

And many the on-coming [troop of horse], like flocks of sand-grouse flying down to the water, that raise high with their hoof-beats the clouds of dark dust,

Have I checked with a steed like a wolf, stout where the heel strikes, long and clean in the legs, a steady galloper when his sides are drenched with sweat,

And with a tawny spear of al-Khatt, whose blade shines like a fire of dry thorn-bushes on which I have heaped fresh fuel so that it blazes up.

And many the true-hearted comrades I have plied with the morning draught of strong wine, what time the cock crowed shrilly in the darkness of night —

Wine that glides smoothly down the gullet, tawny, unmixed, while their hands pass from one to the other morsels of flesh roasted hastily on hot stones,

And wine mixed with water .of which the bubbles leap to the surface, what time the warbling singer is filled full therewith.

And many the troop of pasturing camels, what time the coward choked with his spittle, have I protected, when the crier called loudly for help time after time ;

And many the watching-place I have mounted as the evening drew on, like as the falcon takes up his place to watch for the prey,

As the scout of an army or of a troop of horse assembled for a foray, what time a weakling tribesman cannot captain his men ;

And when the darkness cleared away I sent them forth on their errand — he that looked on them would liken them to a pack of famished wolves.

When the troop rises to a rough upland plain, it pares away with its hoofs its highest parts ; and when it goes down to the low ground, it stirs up about itself a canopy of dust ;

And they ceased not until their spears brought home booty of captives and a herd of camels like red hills from a place far away.

[Yea, I am one of a tribe whose lances in war are to their foes a poison mingled with their meat ;]

Skilled are they in raids : their prey escapes not their horsemen, what time fright paralyses the coward who cannot bestride a steed.

Yea, we gave the men of Farir and Buhtur to drink, with every band of ours, the spear-head and the part of the shaft entering therein — .

And Ma'n too ; and of the two tribes of Jadllah our horse left 'Amirah and as-Sillakhm fallen headlong, smitten with the sword.

And on the Day of Jurad our spears made dead meat of Yazid — and there had not passed by us a gazelle with one horn broken.

And the son of Hisn spent the summer heats in our tents a captive, tending the sores caused by the thongs of leather with the hair on with which his arms were bound.

And of the rider of Mardud our spears distributed the flesh [as it were a slaughtered camel], and they left Mas'ud a prey for hyaenas and wolves.
